</div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkletl-l-ju/" target="_blank" >Chaz Ebert carries Roger’s legacy – and walks her own path</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkletl-l-tl/" target="_blank" >Erica Thompson</a></h5><p>Chaz Ebert is still in love with the movies.</p><p>One of the first to arrive at the Chicago International Film Festival this year, she remained a constant presence, winding through crowds and taking in several screenings she said inspired her to continue efforts and conversations she used to share with her late husband, famed Sun-Times film critic Roger Ebert.</p><p>Chaz oversees several enterprises in honor of her late spouse. That includes the Roger and Chaz Ebert Foundation and the criticism website <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkletl-l-tr/" target="_blank" >rogerebert.com</a>.</p><p>She spends her days approving projects, such as the fundraising campaign for a life-sized, bronze sculpture of Ebert's iconic partner-in-criticism, Gene Siskel. There is also a documentary, play and biopic in the works about the friends — and sometimes foes — who taped their first TV review show more than 50 years ago.</p><p>But Chaz is also leaning into her own creative and charitable pursuits. In recent years, she has directed a short documentary, penned a book, and in 2027, she will host an event honoring inspirational leaders. And she helps fund the Chicago International Film Festival's Black Perspectives program celebrating films by African Americans and those throughout the African diaspora. She's also writing a musical about the Virgin Mary.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkletl-l-ty/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>PICTURE entries.title: White Sox add free-agent right-hander Dustin May to bolster starting rotation
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox are not done adding former Milwaukee Brewers this offseason, but this signing might get more attention than <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/29/white-sox-hiring-matt-roffe-away-from-brewers-to-fill-open-amateur-scouting-director-role" target="_blank" ><u>a new amateur scouting director</u></a>.</p><p>A source confirmed to the Sun-Times that the Sox are signing 29-year-old right-hander Dustin May to a three-year, $52.5 million contract, following their strongly stated need to add starting pitching this winter. May has cleared over 130 innings each of the past two seasons, after injuries slowed the early portions of a career that began as a revered Dodgers pitching prospect.</p><p>Averaging nearly 97 mph with his fastball and generating above-average extension off the mound, the six-foot-six May is still a physical marvel who displays the tools that made him a consensus top-25 prospect in the sport ahead of the 2020 season. Confoundingly for a man who is set to receive the largest free-agent outlay the White Sox have extended in the last four years, the on-field results have lagged behind.</p><p>After missing the 2024 season recovering from Tommy John surgery revision and an esophageal tear, May has posted a 4.85 ERA over the past two years; split across four teams since he’s been dealt midseason two trade deadlines in a row. This August, May was dealt to the Brewers and stayed in their rotation throughout their World Series run, but undeniably struggled. He recorded a 5.65 ERA in 36 ⅔ innings during the regular season after the trade, and allowed seven earned runs in 11 innings of postseason work, including a memorable three-run homer he yielded to Shohei Ohtani in the National League Championship Series.</p><p>May has allowed a .801 OPS to left-handed hitters over the past two seasons, and developing a better off-speed weapon to go alongside his breaking ball-heavy profile is a likely target area for White Sox pitching coaches. Many advanced metrics–and inevitably the Sox’ internal numbers–are far more bullish on the strength of May’s arsenal and command than his results would indicate. In that vein, the right-hander offers the opportunity for a budget-conscious Sox team to land someone with the talent of a mid-rotation starter, at a price discounted by the absence of an above-average full season on his resume.</p><p>But to complete that sort of a coup, the White Sox will have to succeed in getting standout surface-level results out of May where other organizations respected for their pitching development–Brewers, Dodgers, Red Sox–have failed.</p><p>Both Dallas Keuchel ($55.5 million) and Liam Hendriks ($54 million) received slightly higher guarantees, so May will become the owner of the third-largest free-agent contract for a pitcher in White Sox history. He will join a rotation currently heavy on projects and bounce-back candidates behind staff ace Sean Burke. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/11/that-suckers-built-different-grant-taylors-move-to-white-sox-rotation-fits-his-boundary-pushing-style" target="_blank" ><u>Grant Taylor is trying to pull off a conversion</u></a> from relieving last season, Davis Martin is trying to shake off a poor second half worsened by a right calf issue, and Luis Castillo will be trying to redeem the final season of an even larger contract after a career-worst 2026 season.</p><p>If Sox’ run prevention takes the step forward in 2027 that their offense managed in 2026, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/18/white-sox-noah-schultz-hagen-smith-tanner-mcdougal-david-sandlin-brian-bannister-will-venable-erick-fedde-jose-urquidy-davis-martin-al-central" target="_blank" ><u>their pitching development</u></a> will need to carry the day.</p>

entries.title: Downtown and Near North Side District 6a Chicago School Board race too close to call
entries.summary:
District 6a neighborhoods: Near North Side, West Town

The candidate supported by a billionaire-backed political group and charter proponents continued to have a narrow lead over two progressives as of Tuesday, Nov. 17 but the race was too close to call.

With all precincts reporting, around 100 votes separated Isaiah White, a school support worker from Anusha Thotakura, the incumbent who runs a statewide advocacy organization, according to Chicago Board of Election results. Meanwhile, Brenda Lee Anderson, a Northwestern University lecturer on leave, trailed White by just under 1,200 votes.

Election officials have until Nov. 17 to finish counting mail-in ballots and provisional ballots. Final official results are due on Nov. 24.

White said his analysis showed that mail-in ballots historically haven't diverged more than 1% from the pattern of other ballots, which could keep him in the lead. "So, we are cautiously optimistic we will hold our lead, but not taking anything for granted," he said earlier this month. "We are taking everything seriously."

The close race was somewhat unexpected. Voters in the area typically support more conservative candidates. But across the city, candidates supported by the Chicago Teachers Union are doing better than expected after being significantly outspent.

Thotakura got support from the CTU and the Service Employees International Union, which represents school support workers. She seems to be splitting the more left-leaning vote with Anderson, who was not backed by any special interests.

More than $500,000 was spent on White’s campaign by The Urban Center, a centrist political organization that advocates for school choice across public and private schools, and the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools. He also was endorsed by an anti-CTU political action committee that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”

Given its location as part of the commercial and business center of the city, District 6a has just 14 public schools — the fewest of any school board electoral districts — and none are neighborhood high schools. The students who attend Chicago Public Schools here include a more diverse mix than in most districts, but the schools have more white and Asian American students than CPS as a whole.

Two of the schools in the district have the highest rating given by the state; while 60% had the lowest two distinctions, “developing” and “comprehensive,” according to 2026 state data released last week. There are now six levels of designations, up from the five up last year when the bottom two were called “comprehensive” and “intensive.”

Thotakura’s and White’s main priorities are to boost reading and math scores. Anderson’s main goal is to fix CPS’ chronic budget crisis.

Contributing: Reema Amin, Chalkbeat Chicago and Kate Grossman

entries.title: US loses measles elimination status as cases remain low in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>In 2000, the United States was able to officially declare measles eliminated in the country, a hard-fought victory in public health. Twenty six years later, the U.S. can no longer make that claim. </p><p>After years of rising anti-vaccine rhetoric and anti-public health sentiments, the U.S. has suffered several large measles outbreaks. And on Tuesday, a global panel of health experts formally determined that the country has lost "measles elimination status" — meaning the U.S. has gone more than 12 months with uninterrupted transmission of measles. </p><p>"This reflects a complacency that has grown in the last couple decades because people don't see the severity of measles on a day-to-day basis," said Dr. Ravi Jhaveri, the division head of pediatric infectious diseases at Lurie Children’s Hospital.</p><p>"No one should be dying of measles in the U.S.," Jhaveri said. "Not a single person." </p><p>A committee of the Pan American Health Organization, a branch of the World Health Organization, announced their long-anticipated decision Tuesday morning. Mexico also lost its status. </p><p>“Measles elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO’s director. “It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring we reach every community.”</p><p>Measles is a highly contagious virus that starts with a high fever followed by a rash. Most people are able to recover, but it's one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization.</p><p>The last two years have been among the worst for measles in the U.S. with more than 7,000 cases and 11 deaths. Most of the people infected were either unvaccinated or didn't share if they'd had the vaccine. </p><p>While outbreaks have pummeled several states, Illinois continues to see a low count of measles cases. So far in 2026, <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/topics-services/diseases-and-conditions/measles.html" target="_blank" >29 cases have been reported</a> to the Illinois Department of Public Health. No one has died from the virus or been hospitalized this year. Cook County has only one reported case so far this year. Downstate Douglas County has reported the most with 11 cases.</p><p>But in previous years, Illinois has reported single-digit case counts or no cases at all.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-3d0000" name="html-embed-module-3d0000"></a><div style="min-height:438px" id="datawrapper-vis-rL1ub"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/rL1ub/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-rL1ub"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/rL1ub/full.png" alt="Number of measles cases per year in Illinois (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Over 5,700 cases have been reported nationwide in 2026, according to <a class="Link" href="https://publichealth.jhu.edu/ivac/resources/us-measles-tracker" target="_blank" >state and county health department data compiled by Johns Hopkins</a>. Over 1,500 cases have been found in Pennsylvania alone. </p><p>Illinois' rate for the two-dose measles vaccine is holding steady among school-aged children, according to data from the Illinois State Board of Education. For the 2025-2026 school year, the state's vaccination rate is 96.8%. Chicago Public Schools rate is 95.7%, an improvement after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/05/08/less-than-half-of-cps-schools-have-herd-immunity-for-measles-state-data-shows" target="_blank" >district saw a dip</a> in vaccinations coming out of the COVID-19 pandemic. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d70000" name="html-embed-module-d70000"></a><div style="min-height:387px" id="datawrapper-vis-BS7QD"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BS7QD/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-BS7QD"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BS7QD/full.png" alt="Measles vaccination rates in Illinois and Chicago Public Schools (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>A vaccination rate of 95% is a benchmark public health experts use to determine whether a community has hit "herd immunity."</p><p>Jhaveri emphasized that most parents are still getting their kids vaccinated and a "small fragment of the population" is forgoing the shot. </p><p>In the Chicago area, "we still do a great job of having most of our children get the two doses of the vaccine," Jhaveri said. "The risk for us locally is not that high. There will still be small clusters, small outbreaks." </p><p><i>Contributing: Associated Press</i> </p>

entries.title: How Jaguars-Bears in Week 13 could be flexed — or not
entries.summary: <p>Whether the NFL flexes the Bears’ game Dec. 6 against the Jaguars into prime time could depend on whether the Texans lose to the Colts on Thursday.</p><p>But there are plenty of other factors that could determine the kickoff time between teams currently 7-2, which is scheduled for noon on Fox. Here’s a breakdown:</p><p>NBC’s “Sunday Night Football” game Dec. 6 is Texans-Steelers. At 6-3, the Steelers are in playoff contention, but the Texans would drop to 3-7 with a loss to the Colts, likely knocking them out of contention. That would open the door for flexing. If the Texans win, the NFL likely would say both teams are contending and keep the game in prime time.</p><p>Some would debate the Texans’ legitimacy in that scenario, but it’s important to remember the point of flexible scheduling: It’s not to put the best game in prime time, it’s to replace a bad game with a better game. Assuming the Texans win, Texans-Steelers wouldn’t be a bad game, and its viewership might be in line with Jaguars-Bears. The Jags don’t exactly move the needle.</p><p>Plus, Jaguars-Bears isn’t the only game with a chance of being flexed in Week 13. The 49ers-Giants game, scheduled for noon on Fox, is a battle of division leaders. Same with Panthers-Vikings, which is set for 3:25 p.m. on CBS. The Bills-Patriots game, also set for 3:25 p.m. on CBS, took a hit with the injury to Pats quarterback Drake Maye.</p><p>Then the question becomes, which games do CBS and Fox protect? Would Fox protect 49ers-Giants over Jags-Bears? Probably. But Fox is guaranteed a number of Bears games each season. Could losing that game mean Bears-Dolphins in Week 14 would move from CBS to Fox? It’s possible.</p><p>It’s not like the Bears or Jaguars need another prime-time game, anyway. The Bears just had three consecutive night games, and after facing the Bears, the Jags will play in prime time in two of the next three weeks.</p><p>That said, the NFL aims to give the best distribution to its biggest games. If Jaguars-Bears stays on Fox, it likely would go to only a third of the country, in competition with 49ers-Giants and Packers-Saints. For a potential matchup of 9-2 teams, it needs more viewership.</p><p>The NFL doesn’t need to make a decision until next Tuesday, and NFL commissioner Roger Goodell has the final say. With every permutation, there’s always wiggle room to give the boss what he wants.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest
